title: A finite type algebra is locally quasi-finite over a polynomial algebra in its fibre dimension
statement: Let $R\to S$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings of finite type [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra], let $\mathfrak q\subset S$ be prime, and let $\mathfrak p\subset R$ be its inverse image. Write $F=S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ for the fibre ring [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime], and $\mathfrak Q=\ker(F\to\kappa(\mathfrak q))$ for the corresponding prime. Suppose the Krull dimension of $\operatorname{Spec}F$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum] at $\mathfrak Q$ [def-kun-topological-dimension-at-point] is an integer $n\ge0$. Then there are $g\in S\setminus\mathfrak q$ and an $R$-algebra homomorphism $R[t_1,\dots,t_n]\to S_g$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring, def-weil-ring-localization-away] which is quasi-finite: it is of finite type and quasi-finite at every prime of $S_g$ in the sense of [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime].

proof.text: Set $k=\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ and $F=S\otimes_Rk$. This is a finite type $k$-algebra: if $x_1,\ldots,x_N$ generate $S$ over $R$, their images generate $F$ over $k$ [lem-weil-pbc-quasi-finite-four-rings]. The prime $\mathfrak Q$ exists by [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-ring-primes-bijection], so $F\ne0$. By the definition of dimension at a point [def-kun-topological-dimension-at-point], choose an open neighbourhood $U$ of $\mathfrak Q$ in $\operatorname{Spec}F$ of dimension exactly $n$: dimensions of open neighbourhoods are integers at least $n$, and one attains their infimum $n$. Basic opens form a basis, so take $D(a)$ with $\mathfrak Q\in D(a)\subseteq U$. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-ring-localization-quotient], each $a\in F$ can be written as the image of $s\in S$ divided by an element of $R\setminus\mathfrak p$, which is a unit of $F$; hence $D(a)=D(\bar s)$. Choose $g_0=s\notin\mathfrak q$. The localization $F_{\bar g_0}=S_{g_0}\otimes_Rk$ has spectrum $D(\bar g_0)$, of dimension at most $n$ because it is contained in $U$, and at least $n$ because it is an open neighbourhood of $\mathfrak Q$. Thus its dimension is exactly $n$.

source.place: Proof of Lemma 00QE, first paragraph, lines 31183-31198; Remark 00E6, label remark-fundamental-diagram

proof.text: Put $T=S_{g_0}\otimes_Rk$; it is nonzero, finite type over $k$ and has Krull dimension $n$ (step 1). Apply [lem-weil-pbc-noether-normalization-field] to get an injective finite $k$-algebra map $k[Y_1,\ldots,Y_d]\to T$; [lem-zl-noether-normalization-dimension] gives $d=\dim T=n$. Let $y_i$ be the image of $Y_i$. Write each $y_i$ as $s_i/g_0^{e_i}\otimes 1/u_i$ with $s_i\in S$ and $u_i\in R\setminus\mathfrak p$, using the localization description of $T$ [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-ring-localization-quotient]. Replace $y_i$ by $y_i'=(u_i/1)y_i=s_i/g_0^{e_i}\otimes1$. Scaling variables by the nonzero scalars $u_i/1\in k$ is an automorphism of $k[Y_1,\ldots,Y_n]$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring], so the subalgebra $k[y_1',\ldots,y_n']$ equals $k[y_1,\ldots,y_n]$ and $T$ remains finite over it. The elements $s_i/g_0^{e_i}\in S_{g_0}$ therefore define an $R$-algebra map $A=R[t_1,\ldots,t_n]\to S_{g_0}$ whose base change along $R\to k$ is finite. The source's stronger choice from the integer polynomial subalgebra is unnecessary for these lifts.

source.place: Proof of Lemma 00QE, second paragraph, lines 31200-31210, invoking Noether normalization Lemma 00OY; the scalar-rescaling argument makes its lifting clause explicit

proof.text: Let $\mathfrak q_0=\mathfrak qS_{g_0}$ and $P=A^{-1}(\mathfrak q_0)$. The fibre ring of $A\to S_{g_0}$ at $P$ is $C=S_{g_0}\otimes_A\kappa(P)\cong T\otimes_{k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]}\kappa(P)$: the contraction $P\cap R=\mathfrak p$ makes $\kappa(P)$ a $k[t]$-algebra, and the two tensor products impose the same $R$- and $t_i$-relations. Since $T$ is a finite $k[t]$-module (step 2), $C$ is finite-dimensional over $\kappa(P)$. By [lem-weil-pbc-finite-dim-algebra-artinian], $C$ is Artinian. Every prime of $C$ is maximal: its quotient is a finite-dimensional domain over a field, so multiplication by each nonzero element is injective and hence surjective, making the quotient a field. Thus $\dim\operatorname{Spec}C=0$; [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-dim-zero-artinian] makes its spectrum discrete. In particular the prime of $C$ corresponding to $\mathfrak q_0$ is isolated, so $A\to S_{g_0}$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q_0$ [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime]. It is finite type: the original generators of $S$ over $R$, together with $g_0^{-1}$, generate $S_{g_0}$ over $A$ [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra].

source.place: Proof of Lemma 00QE, second paragraph, lines 31208-31212 ('In particular, S is quasi-finite ... at q'); the finite-fibre and isolated-point argument is written out

proof.text: By [lem-weil-pbc-ring-quasi-finite-locus-open] applied to $A\to S_{g_0}$ and $\mathfrak q_0$, choose $h\in S_{g_0}\setminus\mathfrak q_0$ such that $A\to(S_{g_0})_h$ is quasi-finite at every prime. Write $h=b/g_0^m$ with $b\in S\setminus\mathfrak q$ and put $g=g_0b\notin\mathfrak q$. There is a canonical $A$-algebra isomorphism $(S_{g_0})_h\cong S_g$: both localizations invert $g_0$ and $b$, and $g_0b$ is invertible exactly when both factors are. Under this isomorphism the map $A\to S_g$ is finite type (the old generators and $g^{-1}$ generate it) and quasi-finite at every prime, as required.
